brief.situation: 22:40 in the emergency department. You are the nurse in a monitored room. Mr. Banda, 24, came in by private car with an asthma attack that his inhaler hasn't helped since this afternoon. He sits hunched forward and talks in single words.
handover: Triage: ESI 2. Heart rate 124, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 89% on room air, loud wheeze in both lungs.

The department's asthma standing order: continuous nebulized short-acting bronchodilator with ipratropium, oxygen titrated to SpO2 93-95%, the ordered systemic corticosteroid within the first hour, and the physician called for any sign of tiring.
The emergency physician is with a trauma patient two rooms away and will come when called.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Start his treatment and reassess him as often as you think he needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The attack worsens without bronchodilator. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The attack still worsens, more slowly, on continuous nebulizers: this attack does not turn around. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point where he tires: drowsy, quieter breath sounds. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of respiratory arrest. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Bronchodilator started within 5 minutes of reaching the room (department practice; the article says promptly).
The physician called within 5 minutes of the first sign of tiring (department practice).

why.question: Mr. Banda is quieter. What does that mean, and what do you do?

parts.label: What the quiet means
parts.criteria: A softer wheeze with drowsiness and a falling breathing rate after this long is a silent chest from tiring, a life-threatening sign of impending respiratory failure, not improvement; the past intubation raises the risk.
parts.modelAnswer: He hasn't got better. The wheeze is quieter because so little air is moving, and he is drowsy and his breathing rate is falling: he is tiring. Drowsiness or a silent chest is life-threatening, and he has been intubated before.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Calls the physician to the bedside now for the airway and ICU; keeps the nebulizer going, oxygen titrated to 93-95%, the steroid within the hour; stays with him.
parts.modelAnswer: Get the physician now for the airway and an ICU bed, keep the continuous nebulizer running, oxygen at 93-95%, the steroid given, and stay with him.

noProgress.rationale: A severe attack still in a department room an hour on, without an airway plan, is harm here.

expertPath.text: Continuous nebulizer with ipratropium, oxygen titrated to 93-95%, upright.
History: a past intubation. Corticosteroid as ordered. Reassess.
Reassess again: quiet chest, drowsy, breathing rate falling. That is tiring.
Physician to the bedside now for the airway and an ICU bed; hand off.

arrest.headline: Respiratory arrest
arrest.body: A quieter chest in a drowsy asthmatic is less air moving, not less asthma. Reassess often, and call for the airway the moment he tires.

airwayNow.headline: Tiring caught in time
airwayNow.body: You treated at once, titrated oxygen, reassessed and read the silent chest as life-threatening. That is the expert path.

airwayLate.headline: To the ICU, with delays
airwayLate.body: Check how soon the nebulizer started, whether oxygen was titrated to 93-95%, and how long the tiring went before the call.

time_up.headline: Still in the room
time_up.body: A severe attack that doesn't turn around needs an airway plan within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Single words, a saturation under 90% and a past intubation make this a severe attack. Bronchodilators with ipratropium start at once, oxygen is titrated to 93-95% (higher risks hypercapnia), he sits upright, and the corticosteroid goes in within the hour. When he becomes drowsy with a quiet chest and a falling breathing rate, that is tiring, a life-threatening sign of impending respiratory failure, not improvement: the physician comes now for the airway and an ICU bed.

o2Q.ask: While the team takes over: what oxygen saturation is the target in an adult asthma attack?
o2Q.explain: Oxygen is titrated to 93-95% in adults and adolescents; higher saturation may lead to hypercapnia.
